---
title: "Why sweep?"
---

Hyperparameters control the architecture and learning algorithm: for example,
network width, learning rate and training duration. Their effect depends on the
simulation bank, so presets are starting points rather than selected optima.

METIS splits by scenario group: all realizations in a group remain together.
Train weights on training groups, choose settings on validation groups and
reserve test groups for the final selected model. Random group splitting measures
performance under that sampling design; it is not automatically a test of
extrapolation to a new scientific regime.

## A reproducible comparison

1. Fix a bank version, group split, scientific outputs and acceptable error.
2. Choose candidate architectures and a bounded parameter search.
3. Compare original-unit validation metrics shared by the model families.
4. Inspect autonomous trajectories, distributional calibration where relevant,
   and physical constraints, not training loss alone.
5. Evaluate the selected procedure on the independent test bank.

Changing a model changes its training objective, so MSE, flow-matching loss and
negative log density cannot be ranked as though they were the same metric.
If test results drive further development, those groups have become part of
model selection; reserve a new independent test for a final claim.

Use [Hydra multirun](../package/hydra.qmd#sweeps) for local configuration grids,
or [W&B sweeps](sweep-config.qmd) for tracked searches. W&B remains optional;
both routes use the same installed training and artifact code.
